sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
Prior to 1994 most of the investigators considered the Gioia Tauro Plain as a Graben structure, bordered at its eastern margin by the Aspromonte Fault and at its western margin by the horst-like structure of Mount S. Elia. This hypothesis is supported by field reports contemporary to the 1783 earthquake, indicating the formation of a 20 km-long crack running at the base of the presumed Aspromonte Fault and characterised by strong and fresh geomorphic evidence.
Valensise and D'Addezio (1994) first proposed that the Aspromonte Fault is no longer active because no clear evidence of offset deposits can be found and because of inconsistency of the landscape evolution in the Gioia Tauro Plain, that lies in the hangingwall of the fault. Based on the analogy with the nearby source of the 1908 earthquake in the Messina Straits, they proposed that the causative source of the 5 February 1783 earthquake is a relatively young, E-dipping blind normal fault (termed Gioia Tauro Fault) that is progressively generating a syncline having the axis about 5 km inland and parallel to the coast. The same investigators contend that the present shape and elevation of the marine terraces encircling the Plain is best explained by the interplay between regional uplift and more localised bowl-shaped subsidence induced by the activity of the Gioia Tauro Fault.
Later on there have been several attempts to investigate the shape of the filling of the Plain in order to decide whether it is compatible with the action of a steeply-W-dipping or of a gently E-dipping fault. The basin fill turned out to be essentially bowl-shaped, with a maximum thickness of 300-500 m halfway between the Aspromonte piedmont and the present shoreline. This configuration is not compatible with sustained activity of the Aspromonte Fault, which should have induced an half-Graben pattern of sedimentation that is not observed.
The seismicity of the region is very limited and concentrates mostly at the edges of the proposed source. Important geochemical anomalies are also recorded at the northwestern end of the source and have been interpreted as evidence of the interplay between the Gioia Tauro Fault and the transverse structure known as Nicotera-Gioiosa Ionica Line.
Finally, Bosi and Galli (2000) opened a trench across the Aspromonte Fault near Cittanova. They found evidence for recent breaks that they interpret as evidence for primary surface faulting. The quality of the trenched materials (mostly unconsolidated scree at the contact between the crystalline Aspromonte rocks and the basin filling), however, suggests that any surface fractures could be also interpreted in terms of local readjustments due to the ground shaking.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Is there a conclusive test that would settle the dispute between the E-dipping Gioia Tauro Fault and the W-dipping Aspromonte Fault?
2) Could the v-shaped river valleys and the three sets of triangular facets that are used to support the activity of the Aspromonte fault be the result of regional uplift instead of footwall uplift?
3) Could the 20 km-long crack observed by contemporary workers be due to differential behaviour of soft deposits under the seismic action, as suggested by De Dolomieu (1784)?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Cotecchia et al. (1986)
By means of field survey and of analyses of the descriptions provided by numerous chroniclers and scientists sent by the Kingdom of Naples immediately after the event (among the others Grimaldi, 1784; De Dolomieu 1784 and Vivenzio, 1788), they study the geomorphogenic crisis triggered by the February 5, 1783 M7 earthquake. The authors interpret as evidence for surface faulting related to the activation during the 1783 earthquake of the Delianuova-Molochio-Santa Cristina normal fault, a crack running between the village of San Giorgio and of Santa Cristina, which was first described by De Dolomieu. This feature was several feet wide, about 10 miles long, downdropped to the west, and coincided with the contact between the sedimentary sequence outcropping in the Gioia Tauro plain, and the crystalline bedrock forming the Aspromonte Mountain.
They attribute then a great seismogenic potential to this structure.
Tortorici et al. (1986)
On the basis of morphological and structural evidence, they hypothesise that the three shocks occurred on February 5, 6 and 7, 1783 were related to three west-dipping, NE striking high angle normal faults. These faults put in contact the crystalline bedrock forming the Aspromonte and Serre mountains and the Palmi coastal high, with the sedimentary Plio-Pleistocenic clastic sequence outcropping in the Mesima valley and in the Gioia Tauro basin. They also suggest that these faults, together with those with similar strike that exist in the Messina Straits area, may form a right stepping en-echelon array.
Valensise and D'Addezio (1994)
To determine which fault was responsible for the February 5, 1783 earthquake, compare the landscape geomorphological features and geological data and the deformational field produced by two fault geometries both NNE striking but with opposite dip: one low-angle ESE dipping and the other high angle WNW dipping (named the Gioia Tauro Fault and the Aspromonte Fault, respectively. They show that the Gioia Tauro Fault seems to have a geometry more compatible with the overall geological and geomorphological dataset, able to explain the evolution of the Gioia Tauro basin.
Tortorici et al. (1995)
By means of field mapping, structural analysis and morphological observations, they study several normal fault segments that show evidence for Middle Pleistocene to Holocene activity, located along the inner side of the Calabrian Arc. According to these authors these fault segments may be related to the high seismicity typical of the region. In particular, they describe in detail and map the Cittanova Fault, a 15 km-long, NE-striking, high angle normal fault bounding to the east the Gioia Tauro plain. On the basis of morphological and structural analyses, they infer for this structure a very recent activity with prevalent dip slip movement, and an average rate of vertical displacement of about 0.7 mm/yr in the past 120 kyr.
Bosi and Galli (2000)
By merging field and aerial photo survey with archeoseismic investigations they studied the epicentral area of the 5 Feb. 1783 earthquake and conclude that the Cittanova fault (W dipping) is the surface evidence of the seismic source at depth. They locate sites that appear have experienced surface ruptures during that event and excavated trenches at three sites along the Cittanova fault.
Trenches show evidence for paleoearthquakes, dating is underway.

pictures.t: Coastal evolution of Gioia Tauro Plain
pictures.c: Reconstruction of the main terrace inner edges and palaeogeographic evolution of  Gioia Tauro Plain and Messina Straits. Ages are from correlations with global sea-level highstands (from Burrato et al. [1999]).

pictures.t: Block-diagram from Cotecchia et al. [1986]
pictures.c: Cotecchia et al.'s [1986] hypothesis for the surface effects of the 5 February 1783 earthquake. The coseismic ruptures at the foot of the Aspromonte are seen as evidence for primary surface faulting. The geometry of the basin filling is admittedly speculative.

pictures.t: Geological map of Gioia Tauro Plain
pictures.c: Simplified geological map of the Gioia Tauro Plain based on published work (from Valensise and D'Addezio [1994]). SectionA-A' as in figure showing"2D comparison of competing faults".

pictures.t: Geomorphologic map of Gioia Tauro Plain
pictures.c: Geomorphological map of Gioia Tauro Plain showing attitude of recent sediments, dip direction of marine terraces, and terrace inner edges with elevations (from Valensise and D'Addezio [1994]).

pictures.t: Uplift inferred from sedimentology data for the past 0.7 My
pictures.c: Uplift (in mm/y) inferred from sedimentological data averaged over the past 0.7 My. Notice the strong increase in uplift rate after 0.2 Ma (from Ghisetti [1980]).

pictures.t: Regional tectonic sketch from Ghisetti [1984]
pictures.c: Ghisetti [1984] describes both the Gioia Tauro Plain and the Upper Mesima basins as two graben formed by main west-dipping and secondary east-dipping faults, and points out the existence of transverse structures separating individual basins.

pictures.t: Gravimetric profile across Aspromonte foothills
pictures.c: Hypothesis for the geometry of the basin filling resulting from each of the two competing faults, and comparison between the observed gravimetric anomalies and those calculated for the two cases (from Valensise and D'Addezio [1994]).

pictures.t: Gioia Tauro Fault displacement vs drainage
pictures.c: Comparison between the deformation field produced by the Gioia Tauro Fault and the drainage pattern of the Plain: streams belonging to the two main catchments converge toward the area of maximum subsidence (from Cucci et al. [1996]).

pictures.t: Gioia Tauro Fault displacement vs morphology
pictures.c: Match between the low-angle, east-dipping, Gioia Tauro Fault, the attitude of recent sediments (describing a wide syncline centered in the Plain) and the distribution and dip direction of marine terrace inner edges (from D'Addezio et al. [1994]).

pictures.t: Geomorphological map of southern Calabria from Lembke [1931]
pictures.c: German geographer Lembke [1931] first envisioned the western slope of the Aspromonte-Serre Massif as a major west-dipping normal fault.

pictures.t: General scheme from Miyauchi et al. [1994]
pictures.c: Fault geometry and tectonic scheme describing the Early-Middle Pleistocene uplift of Southern Calabria, which is assumed to have generated normal and gravitational faulting (from Miyauchi et al. [1994]).

pictures.t: Calabrian faults from the Neotectonic Map of Italy
pictures.c: The Neotectonic Map of Italy (Ciaranfi et al. [1983]) proposes the existence of a west-dipping, range-bounding normal fault and shows that the whole southern Calabria has been strongly uplifted since the Middle Pleistocene.

pictures.t: Profiles of Petrace and Mesima rivers
pictures.c: Topographic profiles along the Mesima and Petrace rivers.Close to its mouth the Petrace R. is in the footwall of the hypothesized Gioia Tauro Fault and becomes antecedent. Arrows point to terrace inner edges (from Burrato [1995])

pictures.t: Stratigraphic constraints for age of faulting
pictures.c: Section showing that sediments of the Plain are found at higher elevation near the Aspromonte Fault, that is, where modelling of fault-induced vertical displacement predicts maximum subsidence (from Valensise and D'Addezio [1994]).

pictures.t: Subsurface geology from geoelectric/well data
pictures.c: Contours of the base of the upper resistive layer (Holocene continental deposits) of the sequence filling the Gioia Tauro basin: notice the location of a depocenter halfway between the range and the coastline (from Burrato et al. [1999]).

pictures.t: Map from Suess [1874]
pictures.c: Geologic structure of the Aspromonte Range and adjacent Gioia Tauro Plain according to Suess [1874]. The Aspromonte crystalline rocks are uncomformably overlain by young Tertiary clastics along the "Peripherische Linie".

pictures.t: Cittanova-Delianuova range front
pictures.c: Detailed morphotectonic map of the Aspromonte foothills between Cittanova and Delianuova, showing three generations of faceted spurs interpreted by Tortorici et al. [1995] as evidence for active normal faulting.

pictures.t: Seismotectonic sketch of southern Calabria [Tortorici et al., 1995]
pictures.c: Seismotectonic sketch of southern Calabria showing the hypothesized sources for the entire 1783 earthquake sequence (from Tortorici et al. [1995]).

pictures.t: Cross-section from Westaway [1993]
pictures.c: Expected profiles of tilting of the Gioia Tauro Plain resulting from slip on the inferred Aspromonte Fault. Profile 3 is preferred and is believed to approximate the bottom of the basin fill, not constrained by subsurface data (from Westaway [1993]).

pictures.t: 2D comparison of competing faults
pictures.c: Sections showing competing faults (A), the associated surface vertical displacements (B), compared with topography (C) and subsurface geometry of the upper layer of sedimentary sequence (D) (from Burrato et al.[1999]).

pictures.t: Aspromonte Fault displacements
pictures.c: Comparison between expected tilt for Aspromonte Fault, dip direction of  terraces and recent sediments (left), and mean drainage direction (right). The fault causes attraction of  drainage towards the Aspromonte (SE) (from Valensise and D'Addezio [1994]).

pictures.t: Schematic section [Tiberti et al., 2017]
pictures.c: Schematic section of the fault systems in the general context of the active Calabrian W-dipping subduction (from Tiberti et al. [2017]).

pictures.t: Overview of the sources [Tiberti et al., 2017]
pictures.c: Overview of the Calabrian sources. Notice that 1. the main normal faults lie antithetic to the subduction plane and host the largest earthquakes, and 2. between 1783 and 1908 large earthquakes ruptured the western extensional domain of the Southern Calabria (from Tiberti et al. [2017]).
